    What is the meaning of crown?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    A dental crown is a custom-made "cap" that fully covers a damaged, weak, or decayed tooth to restore its shape, strength, and function. It is permanently cemented over the visible portion of the tooth above the gum line. Crowns are commonly used after root canals, to fix broken teeth, or to cover dental implants. 
    Key Details About Dental Crowns 
    • Purpose: Crowns strengthen weak teeth, prevent cracked teeth from breaking further, and improve the appearance of misshapen or discolored teeth.
    • Materials: They are made from various materials, including porcelain, ceramic, metal alloys (like gold), or porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM)
      .
    • Procedure: The process generally requires two visits: first to prepare the tooth and place a temporary, and second to fit the permanent, custom-made crown.
    • Lifespan: With proper care, dental crowns can last between five and 15 years.
    • Alternatives: If only part of the tooth is damaged, a dentist might recommend an inlay or onlay rather than a full crown.

      History. What is the history of the crown?
      About this result

      AI Overview
      The history of the crown spans from ancient wreaths symbolizing triumph to complex medieval and modern regalia representing sovereign power, evolving from simple bands to jeweled structures with arches, notably changing after the English Civil War when older items were melted down and replaced with elaborate new ones like St. Edward's Crown and the Imperial State Crown, serving as symbols of authority in coronations and state events.
       
      Ancient Origins & Early Symbols
      • Wreaths: Early forms of crowns were wreaths of laurel, myrtle, or celery given as rewards for athletes and warriors, as seen in Classical times. 
      • Diadems: Browbands like the diadem, worn by Achaemenid Persian emperors, became symbols of royalty, adopted by Roman emperors.
      • Egyptian Crowns: Pharaohs wore distinctive crowns like the double crown (Pschent) and the Khepresh (blue war crown). 
      Medieval Evolution (England)
      • Helmets: Early English kings were invested with helmets, not crowns, with the chief barbarian wearing a distinctive helmet.
      • Wreath-like Crowns: These evolved into circlets of jewels, leading to the addition of upstanding ornaments to distinguish royal crowns.
      • Edward the Confessor (11th Century): His seal shows him with a helmet, but he's associated with the regalia deposited at Westminster Abbey, a precursor to the Crown Jewels. 
      • William the Conqueror: Crowned with a simple gold coronet. 
      The Crown Jewels & Destruction
      • Medieval Regalia: A collection of royal ornaments was assembled by Edward the Confessor.
      • English Civil War (1649): Oliver Cromwell ordered the medieval regalia to be broken up and sold, as symbols of monarchy.
      • Restoration (1660s): New regalia, including St. Edward's Crown, were made for Charles II, incorporating some surviving pieces like the Coronation Spoon. 
      Modern British Crowns (Examples)
      • St. Edward's Crown (1661): Made for Charles II, it's used for the crowning moment in the coronation. 
      • Imperial State Crown (1838/1937): Created for Victoria (later modified), it's lighter and worn as the monarch leaves the Abbey and for State Openings of Parliament, containing famous gems like the Black Prince's Ruby and Cullinan II diamond. 
      The Concept of "The Crown"
      • Feudal System: In England, "The Crown" became a legal entity representing the monarch's powers and privileges, separate from the person of the monarch.
      • Imperial Crown: Defined under Henry VIII, asserting England's sovereignty.
      • Commonwealth: The concept extended to the UK's dependencies and Commonwealth realms.
